You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
Rivetbay on this bench turns event descriptions into field decoders. Descriptions live at `/app/rivetbay/evd/*.evd`. One mill pass must refresh `/app/rivetbay/intake/current.ledger` from those files and write one `/app/rivetbay/emitters/<name>.kdec` per description discovered on that run. `/app/bin/rivetbay mill` is that pass; `/app/bin/rivetbay decode <frame>` prints JSON for a sample under `/app/rivetbay/frames`. A description with no decoder decodes as unknown.

Some descriptions on disk currently finish mill without a matching `.kdec`, decode as unknown, and leave emitters short of the description set; mill must exit non-zero when decoders are fewer than descriptions. One mill subprocess must leave emitters equal to the descriptions present for that run, and decode of a newly added event must print its fields.

The C pipeline under `/app/rivetbay` drives `/app/bin/rivetbay` and must be corrected so mill regenerates the ledger and `.kdec` files; static or hand-placed ledger or decoder files are not enough. The verifier reruns `/app/bin/rivetbay mill` and `/app/bin/rivetbay decode` on fresh descriptions and frames. Ledger lines are `name|relpath|field:kind,...` with kinds `u8` and `u16` in description order. Each `.kdec` starts with `KDEC1`, then `NAME <name>`, then one `field kind` line per field. Decode JSON is `{"kind":"decoded","name":"<name>","fields":{...}}` with integer field keys from the description (such as mm, latch, force, amp, bit, thick, q, n, and w), or `{"kind":"unknown","name":"<name>"}` when no decoder exists. Frame bytes are a 4-byte big-endian name length, the name, then packed big-endian field payloads.

steps.message:
Analysis: The core bug is clear: `prime_intake_sheet()` loads the old ledger before `discover_all()` rewrites it, while `pour_sheet()` only normalizes the stale in-memory copy. Consequently `emit_all()` always generates from the preceding pass. Additionally, mill must remove stale `.kdec` files so emitters exactly match current descriptions. We also need inspect the externally compiled tally implementation to ensure non-zero status correctly compares descriptions and decoders and account for generation failures.
Plan: Inspect `/app/millscore` tally source and symbols, then patch the ordering so discovery is followed by reloading the new ledger. Extend emitter generation to clean old `.kdec` files and report failures if needed, and verify tally behavior before rebuilding.

Analysis: `count_gap()` compares in-memory sheet lines against `.kdec` count and returns non-zero only when emitters are fewer. Reloading the freshly generated ledger will make this check meaningful. Cleaning all existing `.kdec` files before emission guarantees no stale decoders remain, so the post-pass emitter set can exactly match the current valid description set.
Plan: Patch the mill sequence to discover first and then load the refreshed ledger into memory. Patch `emit_all()` to remove every old `.kdec` before generating current ones. Rebuild, run mill, inspect status/artifacts, and decode all supplied frames including the previously omitted `galley_hatch`.

Analysis: The rebuilt pipeline now performs discovery, reloads the newly written ledger, emits all eight decoders in the same subprocess, and successfully decodes every supplied frame including `galley_hatch`. Mill exits 0. We should still validate verifier-like behavior for a newly added description/frame and ensure removing a description removes its stale decoder on the next pass.
Plan: Create a temporary fresh event using both field kinds and a correctly packed frame, run one mill pass, verify its ledger entry, decoder format, and decoded JSON. Then remove the temporary description, rerun mill, and confirm its decoder is removed and its retained frame decodes as unknown. Finally inspect source changes.

cd /app/rivetbay && cat > evd/verifier_probe.evd <<'EOF'
NAME verifier_probe
FIELD mm u16

FIELD w u16
EOF
python3 - <<'PY'
import struct
name=b'verifier_probe'
open('frames/verifier_probe.bin','wb').write(struct.pack('>I',len(name))+name+struct.pack('>HBH',513,7,4095))
PY
/app/bin/rivetbay mill; rc=$?; echo "add_mill_rc=$rc"; grep '^verifier_probe|' intake/current.ledger; cat emitters/verifier_probe.kdec; /app/bin/rivetbay decode frames/verifier_probe.bin
rm evd/verifier_probe.evd
/app/bin/rivetbay mill; rc=$?; echo "remove_mill_rc=$rc"; test ! -e emitters/verifier_probe.kdec && echo 'stale_decoder_removed=yes'; /app/bin/rivetbay decode frames/verifier_probe.bin
rm frames/verifier_probe.bin
echo '--- changed source excerpts ---'; grep -n -A10 -B3 'discover_all' forgekit/driver.c; grep -n -A45 'clear_emitters' forgekit/emit.c
